past_actions.summary: Price and pursue bid on a two-car garage addition — largest single job this year if awarded. Spend evening reviewing material costs and labor hours to sharpen the estimate.
past_actions.emotional_state: Grounded, confident, mildly ambitious. The kind of quiet satisfaction a man gets when the work is there, the savings are real, and he still enjoys the job. No anxiety. The truck started this morning on the first crank, like it always does.

past_actions.summary: Prioritize closing the Henderson garage addition bid before Phase 2 RoboRide deployment creates uncertainty in the Auto Row economy. Push for a signed contract within 30 days rather than letting it drift.
past_actions.emotional_state: Calm and slightly alert. Not rattled — the truck panic that might hit another person is entirely absent. But there is a low-grade unease about the people downstream. The kind of unease a contractor gets when he hears a big local employer is 'evaluating options.' He's done this long enough to know that threat usually travels one hop further than people expect.

past_actions.summary: Reach out through my professional network — Carlos the mechanic, community organizer Lisa Freeman, and other contractors I know — to get a read on who still has work and what projects are still being planned. Use these conversations to position myself as available and reliable before the competition gets desperate. Also follow up on the Henderson bid with a direct call, offering to hold material pricing for 60 days to give them a reason to commit now rather than wait.

Call Henderson directly to push for a decision on the garage addition bid. Make clear the 60-day material price hold is still in effect but not indefinite — frame it as a favor I can only extend a bit longer. If they are not ready to commit, ask directly what is holding them back and whether a phased start date helps.

Accept that Henderson is cooling and shift focus — send one final, brief written note to Henderson letting them know the material price hold expires in two weeks and the bid will need to be repriced after that. No pressure, no follow-up call. Put the ball firmly in their court and move on mentally. I have spent five ticks on this. It either comes in or it does not.

Make a decision on health insurance. After five ticks of avoidance and one tick of acknowledging the gap, actually commit to enrolling the family in a mid-tier marketplace plan. The math is brutal but it is also clear: $1,400 a month hurts. A $60,000 hospitalization without coverage destroys the savings runway entirely. Three dependents. Dale is 50 and does physical labor. He cannot carry this risk indefinitely and tell himself it is acceptable. Complete the application on the state marketplace, select a plan, and submit. Expense goes up by approximately $1,400 a month. Savings accumulation drops from roughly $900 a month to a deficit position. But the savings buffer at $51,863 can absorb this while income holds. This is not a comfortable decision. It is the right one.

reflections.reflection: I spent five ticks chasing the Henderson garage addition bid like it was the only job in Millfield. It was a good bid — the largest single job of the year — and I do not regret pursuing it hard. But the spending index just hit 48. Nearly one in four people here is out of work. People do not add garages when they are scared they cannot make rent. I should have started diversifying my pipeline three ticks ago when the signals first came in. I did not because the Henderson bid felt real and close. That is normalcy bias. I know what it costs and I paid it again.
reflections.identity_shift: Still Dale Cooper. Still a contractor. The truck is still my identity and I am not selling it or retraining at 50. But I am accepting that working alone without a diversified bid book is a liability, not a virtue. I am a skilled tradesman in a scared economy and I need to act like it — lean, active, building relationships, not waiting on one customer.
regrets: Did not start pricing smaller jobs in ticks 3 or 4 when the macro signals first showed up. Let one big bid crowd out the whole pipeline for too long.
Should have had the Lisa Freeman conversation two ticks earlier — she responded warmly, which means she was receptive. I left value on the table by treating her as a backup contact.
successes: Kept stress low and savings growing through a genuinely deteriorating local economy. Runway is still solid.
Made the Henderson call in tick 5 rather than letting it drift — even if it does not close, I acted with directness and professionalism.
Reached out to Lisa Freeman proactively before I needed the help. That goodwill is already in motion.
Did the financial scenario planning in tick 5 — I know my number. That is not nothing.
reflections.adaptation_notes: Shift from single-bid focus to active multi-bid pipeline. Smaller jobs, needs-based work (roofs, drainage, foundations), not luxury additions. Use the Lisa Freeman relationship as an intelligence channel for community and nonprofit construction projects. Stop waiting for Henderson and start filling the calendar with what is actually available. The market is telling me something. This time I am listening before it gets worse.
